title_en: Zhang Jing v. Yu Lingfeng — dispute over infringement of reputation rights in the online environment
keywords_en: civil; dispute over right to reputation; first instance; primary people's court; Jiangsu Province; natural person; General Principles of the Civil Law; whether online virtual identities have right to reputation; determination of online tortious acts; proof of identity of the tortfeasor; in favor of plaintiff; insulting online posts; acquaintance through online friend gatherings; matching online pseudonyms to real identities; right to reputation; dispute over infringement of right to reputation in the online environment
full_text_en:
Zhang Jing v. Yu Lingfeng — dispute over infringement of reputation rights in an online environment

Plaintiff: Zhang Jing, female, 21 years old, Shanghai Chief Representative of Nanjing Dianjin Planning Co., Ltd. of Jiangsu Province, residing in Xuanwu District, Nanjing.

Agent ad litem: Zhang Min, lawyer of Nanjing United Law Firm, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: Yu Lingfeng, male, 26 years old, graphic designer of Nanjing Baishengli Advertising Company, Jiangsu Province, residing at West Beijing Road, Nanjing.

Agent ad litem: Zhu Weizhong, lawyer of Guotai Xinhua Law Firm, Jiangsu Province.

The plaintiff Zhang Jing, due to a dispute with the defendant Yu Lingfeng over infringement of reputation rights in an online environment, initiated an action with the Gulou District People's Court of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.

Plaintiff's Allegations: The plaintiff is a netizen, using the online pseudonym Hongyanjing. On the Nanjing Xici Hutong website, both her real name and online pseudonym have a certain degree of visibility. At a netizen gathering, through introduction by others, the plaintiff met the defendant Yu Lingfeng and learned that his online pseudonym was Huarongdao. After March 4, 2001, the defendant used the online pseudonym Da Yue Jin to post several messages insulting the plaintiff's personality on the internet, infringing upon the plaintiff's reputation rights. The plaintiff requests that the court order the defendant to cease the infringement, eliminate its effects, offer an apology, and pay the plaintiff RMB 10,000 as compensation for mental distress.

The defendant did not submit a written defense, but during the proceedings argued: The user of a registered ID (identity authentication) is not unique. A virtual ID can be used by multiple users; any person who goes online can log in using that identity as long as they have the password. Posting messages on the internet under the pseudonym Da Yue Jin does not necessarily indicate that it was done by the defendant; there exists the possibility that the defendant's password was stolen. Although the plaintiff's pseudonym Hongyanjing has visibility on the Xici Hutong website, that does not mean the plaintiff has influence in society. Attacks between virtual entities on the internet should be a matter of morality and website regulations. Virtual IDs only affect the virtual online society and do not affect the evaluation of the reputation of real persons in real society. Virtual entities on the internet do not have personality rights and are not protected by law. The defendant has not infringed upon the plaintiff's reputation rights.

The Gulou District People's Court of Nanjing found the following facts upon trial:

The plaintiff Zhang Jing registered on the eLong Xici Hutong website under the pseudonym Hongyanjing and moderated and managed a discussion board. The defendant Yu Lingfeng registered on the same website under the pseudonym Huarongdao. Both Hongyanjing and Huarongdao were registered as genuine netizen level on the Xici Hutong website. On November 19, 2000, the "Under Purple Mountain" discussion board and the "One Red Thread" discussion board on the Xici Hutong website organized a netizen gathering. Through the gathering, netizens came to know each other and learned each other's online pseudonyms used when online. In addition to participating in activities of genuine netizens under the pseudonym Huarongdao, Yu Lingfeng also registered on the eLong Xici Hutong website under the pseudonym Da Yue Jin, with a level of registered netizen on that website.

On March 4, 2001, on a relevant discussion board of the eLong Xici Hutong website, a netizen using the pseudonym Da Yue Jin published an article titled "Remembering Hongyanjing Who Lost Red-Eyed Yesterday". In the article, when describing Hongyanjing winning or losing cards, insulting language such as "beating chest and stamping feet, wailing as if bereaved of parents, throwing tantrums, cursing, and cornered beasts jumping over the wall" was used. On March 7, Da Yue Jin published an article titled "I Am Huarongdao, and I Have an Affair with Hongyanjing". On April 30, Da Yue Jin also published an article titled "Bayonet Stabbed into the Soft Ribs of [Little Pig Loneliness]". The article contained language such as "The soft ribs referred to in this article are a scarlet woman pointed at by a thousand people, a wanton cyber-courtesan; a spokesperson for cyber-porn venues; the malformed product of the severe gender imbalance among Chinese netizens — Hongyanjing." From May 8 to May 9, Da Yue Jin repeated the above insulting language in follow-up posts online. On May 29, in a post titled "I Oppose Malicious Speculation on the 'Cross-Linear Sexual Harassment' Incident!", Da Yue Jin used language such as "This reminds me of this fake virgin Hongyanjing..." On May 31, in an article titled "Hongyanjing! You Dare Touch a Finger of Mine, You'll Bear All Consequences!", Da Yue Jin stated, "You neither can go out to earn money, nor can you fight for your brothers. If you were reborn as a male, at best you'd be a kept man." The click-through rates for the above posts ranged from dozens to hundreds.

Separately found, on March 4, 2001, the plaintiff Zhang Jing, in response to the article published under the pseudonym Da Yue Jin, also published an article titled "Da Yue Jin = Huarongdao" on the "Infinite Contact" discussion board of the eLong Xici Hutong website under her pseudonym Hongyanjing. That article was also published on other discussion boards of the Xici Hutong website and contained language attacking Da Yue Jin.

The evidence confirming the above facts includes:

1. The notarized certificate submitted by the plaintiff Zhang Jing for the preservation of evidence of the online articles, which can confirm a series of insulting articles published under the pseudonym Da Yue Jin on the eLong Xici Hutong website.

2. The netizen information and login logs of the Xici Hutong website obtained by the court from Beijing Yilong Information Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yilong Company, also known as eLong online), which can prove that the plaintiff Zhang Jing's pseudonym is Hongyanjing, and she is a genuine netizen; the defendant Yu Lingfeng's pseudonym is Huarongdao, and he is also a genuine netizen; Da Yue Jin is a pseudonym used by a netizen at the registered level.

Based on the timing of the publication of the above articles by Da Yue Jin, the court obtained from the Xici Hutong website the login time periods and IP addresses (internet computer addresses determined according to the International Internet Protocol) of Da Yue Jin and Huarongdao during the period from May 22 to June 21, and through the Jiangsu Provincial Public Multimedia Bureau, found that the calling number of the telephone used for the online logins of Huarongdao and Da Yue Jin was the same, and that calling number was consistent with the telephone number of the defendant Yu Lingfeng's home used for internet access, as admitted by Yu Lingfeng himself. This confirms that the authors of the articles "I Oppose Malicious Speculation on the 'Cross-Linear Sexual Harassment' Incident!" and "Hongyanjing! You Dare Touch a Finger of Mine, You'll Bear All Consequences!" published on the eLong Xici Hutong website under the pseudonym Da Yue Jin on May 29 and May 31 were the defendant Yu Lingfeng in this case.

Yilong Company stipulated that for netizens registered on its website, as long as their password is not stolen by others, others cannot repeatedly log in to the site using the same pseudonym. The notarized certificate proves that from March 4, 2001, to May, articles published under the pseudonym Da Yue Jin on the Xici Hutong website were uninterrupted. From the chain of evidence thus formed, it can be inferred that the Da Yue Jin who published posts concerning Hongyanjing on the eLong Xici Hutong website on March 4, March 7, April 30, and other times was the same person as the Da Yue Jin who published articles concerning Hongyanjing on that website on May 29 and 31, i.e., the defendant Yu Lingfeng in this case.

3. The netizen gathering photos and witness testimony submitted by the plaintiff Zhang Jing, mutually corroborated with the statements of both parties, can prove that Zhang Jing and the defendant Yu Lingfeng came to know each other through the netizen gathering, and Zhang Jing's real identity and the pseudonym she used have become known to others.

The Gulou District People's Court of Nanjing held:

Reputation is the comprehensive evaluation by society of a citizen or legal person's moral character, reputation, image, and so forth. Article 101 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "Citizens and legal persons shall enjoy the right of reputation. The personality of citizens shall be protected by law, and the use of insults, defamation, or other means to damage the reputation of citizens or legal persons shall be prohibited." The right of reputation of citizens is protected by law, and no one may use any form to insult or damage another's reputation.

The internet is a product of technological development and has an inestimable role in promoting the progress of human society. Although cyberspace is virtual, the human behavior reflected through every action taken online is real. Article 6, paragraph 2 of the "Decision on Safeguarding Internet Security" adopted by the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress stipulates: "Where the internet is used to infringe upon the lawful rights and interests of others, constituting a civil tort, civil liability shall be borne according to law." Cyberspace, as a medium of modern society for disseminating information and communication, is even more so a healthy and orderly space for activities. It should be regulated by morality and constrained by law, and must never be allowed to develop into a tool for some people to do as they please. Using the internet to insult others or fabricate facts to defame others, infringing upon the lawful rights and interests of others and constituting a tort, shall give rise to civil liability.

In this case, although the plaintiff Zhang Jing and the defendant Yu Lingfeng each logged into the website and participated in its activities using virtual pseudonyms, in real life, through the gathering, they came to know each other and knew the real persons corresponding to the pseudonyms. Moreover, Zhang Jing's pseudonym Hongyanjing and her real identity were also known to other netizens. Hongyanjing was no longer merely a virtual identity online. Among netizens who knew each other's real identities, although they continued to communicate online using pseudonyms, such communication was no longer confined to virtual cyberspace, and the object of communication was no longer a virtual person, but had become realistic and targeted. Yu Lingfeng, through the public discussion boards of the Xici Hutong website, published several statements under the pseudonym Da Yue Jin targeting Hongyanjing, i.e., Zhang Jing, and on multiple occasions used insulting language to demean the personality of Hongyanjing, i.e., Zhang Jing. Subjectively, Yu Lingfeng had the malice to damage Zhang Jing's reputation. Objectively, he committed acts that infringed upon Zhang Jing's right of reputation, inevitably affecting the fair evaluation of Zhang Jing by others. He shall bear civil liability for the tort.

Article 120, paragraph 1 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "If a citizen's right of personal name, right of portrait, right of reputation, or right of honor is infringed upon, the victim has the right to demand cessation of the infringement, restoration of reputation, elimination of the effects, and offer of an apology, and may also demand compensation for losses." After the defendant Yu Lingfeng infringed upon the plaintiff Zhang Jing's right of reputation, Zhang Jing's request for him to cease the infringement, eliminate its effects, and offer an apology is legally well-founded and should be supported. Regarding the compensation for mental distress claimed by the plaintiff Zhang Jing, according to the provisions of Article 8, paragraph 2 of the Supreme People's Court's "Interpretation on Several Issues concerning the Determination of Compensation for Mental Damage in Civil Torts", the defendant Yu Lingfeng may be ordered to pay compensation. Considering that the number of people who know that Hongyanjing is Zhang Jing is limited, the actual effects caused by the infringing acts have certain limitations in scope, and taking into account factors such as that Zhang Jing also published inappropriate statements online against Yu Lingfeng after being infringed upon, the request for compensation of RMB 10,000 is not supported. The specific amount of compensation shall be determined by the court at its discretion.

In conclusion, the Gulou District People's Court of Nanjing, on July 16, 2001, rendered the following judgment:

1. The defendant Yu Lingfeng shall cease infringing upon the reputation of the plaintiff Zhang Jing, and within three days from the date this judgment takes effect, shall offer an apology to Zhang Jing on the eLong Xici Hutong website. The content of the apology shall be subject to review by this court. Otherwise, this court will publish the judgment on a national website, and the publication costs shall be borne by Yu Lingfeng.

2. The defendant Yu Lingfeng shall, within three days from the date this judgment takes effect, pay the plaintiff Zhang Jing RMB 1,000 as compensation for mental distress.

Court acceptance fee of RMB 510 and other litigation costs of RMB 1,200 shall be borne by the plaintiff Zhang Jing in the amount of RMB 460 and by the defendant Yu Lingfeng in the amount of RMB 1,250.

After the judgment was pronounced, neither party appealed, and the first-instance judgment became legally effective.
